tracks.name: Base Case & Accumulation
tracks.blurb: The two halves every recursive function needs, and trusting the call to have already solved the smaller problem.

tracks.name: Recursion Meets Structure
tracks.blurb: Nested lists, branching calls, and returning more than one thing at once -- the shapes trees need next.

tracks.name: Strings & Numbers
tracks.blurb: The same two-part shape on new kinds of input: strings, pairs of numbers, and an integer shrinking by division instead of slicing.

tracks.name: New Shapes of Recursion
tracks.blurb: Halving instead of peeling one off, comparing against a lookahead result, choosing to include or exclude, and building up a list of moves instead of a single number.

problems.title: Factorial, the Smallest Possible Recursion
problems.blurb: One base case, one recursive case, nothing else -- get this reflex automatic first.
problems.statement:
Write factorial(n) recursively: n! is n * (n - 1) * ... * 1, and 0! is 1 by definition. Assume n >= 0.

Do not use a loop. The point of this problem is entirely the shape: one line that stops the recursion, one line that trusts factorial(n - 1) to already be correct and builds this call's answer on top of it.
hints: The base case is the smallest input you can answer without recursing at all: n == 0. What is 0! by definition?

For everything else, assume factorial(n - 1) already returns the correct answer for n - 1 -- don't try to trace through what it does internally. Given that trusted number, how do you build n!  from it?
return n * factorial(n - 1). Nothing more is needed.

tests.name: the base case itself
tests.src: assert factorial(0) == 1

tests.name: small values
tests.src:
assert factorial(1) == 1
assert factorial(2) == 2
assert factorial(3) == 6

tests.name: checked against a direct loop

problems.title: Summing a List Without a Loop
problems.blurb: The base case is the empty list -- and the recursive call already solved everything after the first element.
problems.statement:
Write sum_list(values), the sum of a list of numbers, without using a loop or the built-in sum.

The recursive step splits the list into its first element and "everything else": values[0] and values[1:]. Trust that sum_list(values[1:]) already correctly adds up everything after the first element -- don't try to reason about what happens two or three calls deep. Given that trusted number, what do you add to it?
hints: The base case is the empty list -- there is nothing to add, so what should an empty list sum to?
The recursive case: values[0] + sum_list(values[1:]). The slice values[1:] is a brand-new, one-shorter list -- that's what makes the recursion make progress toward the base case.
If you're tempted to write a loop inside this function, stop -- the recursive call is doing the loop's job. Each call handles exactly one element, then delegates the rest.

tests.name: the empty list sums to zero
tests.src: assert sum_list([]) == 0

tests.name: small lists
tests.src:
assert sum_list([5]) == 5
assert sum_list([1, 2, 3, 4]) == 10
assert sum_list([-3, 3]) == 0

tests.name: negative numbers throughout
tests.src: assert sum_list([-1, -2, -3]) == -6

tests.name: random lists, checked against the built-in sum
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(3)
for _ in range(200):
    values = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 12))]
    assert sum_list(values) == sum(values), values

problems.title: The Biggest Number, One Element at a Time
problems.blurb: Compare the first element against what the rest of the list already decided -- not against a value you invent.
problems.statement:
Write max_of_list(values): the largest number in a non-empty list, recursively, without the built-in max.

This is the exact shape a later tree problem needs, so it's worth getting the instinct right here first: the recursive call max_of_list(values[1:]) already correctly tells you the largest value among everything after the first element. Your only job at this call is to compare values[0] against that trusted number.

A list of one element has nothing to compare against and nothing left to recurse into -- that's your base case. Watch for negative numbers: a starting guess of 0 is wrong if every value in the list is negative.
hints: Base case: a list with exactly one element. Its max is that element -- there's nothing to recurse into.

Recursive case: rest_max = max_of_list(values[1:]). That call has already found the biggest value in everything after the first element. Now compare values[0] against rest_max directly -- don't seed a running variable from 0 or from values[0] alone and then loop.
return values[0] if values[0] > rest_max else rest_max.

tests.name: a single element is its own max
tests.src: assert max_of_list([7]) == 7

tests.name: small lists, max in different positions
tests.src:
assert max_of_list([3, 9, 2]) == 9
assert max_of_list([9, 3, 2]) == 9
assert max_of_list([3, 2, 9]) == 9

tests.name: all negative -- zero is not a safe starting guess
tests.src:
assert max_of_list([-5, -1, -9]) == -1
assert max_of_list([-1, -2, -3]) == -1

tests.name: random lists, checked against the built-in max
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(4)
for _ in range(200):
    values = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    assert max_of_list(values) == max(values), values

problems.title: Counting a Value Through Nested Lists
problems.blurb: No fixed depth to loop over -- a list inside a list inside a list, however deep, needs recursion to reach the bottom.
problems.statement:
A list can hold plain numbers and other lists, nested arbitrarily deep: [1, [2, 3, [4]], 5]. Write count_value(nested, target): how many times target appears anywhere inside, at any depth.

There is no way to know the nesting depth ahead of time, so a fixed number of loops can't reach the bottom -- recursion is the only way to handle "arbitrarily deep." This is exactly the shape of a tree's children list, just without a Node class wrapped around it.
hints: Loop over the elements of nested. For each one, check: is this element itself a list, or a plain number?
isinstance(item, list) tells you which case you're in. If item is a list, recurse into it: count_value(item, target). If it isn't, just compare it to target directly.
Keep a running total and add each element's contribution -- either count_value(item, target) for a nested list, or 1 (if it equals target) / 0 (if it doesn't) for a plain number.

tests.name: a flat list
tests.src: assert count_value([1, 2, 3], 2) == 1

tests.name: the empty list
tests.src: assert count_value([], 9) == 0

tests.name: repeats scattered across depths
tests.src: assert count_value([1, [2, 3, [2]], 2], 2) == 3

tests.name: deep nesting, a single match at the bottom
random nested lists, checked against a direct flatten

problems.title: Flattening a Nested List, Lazily
problems.blurb: yield from a recursive call -- the exact tool a tree's leaf-walk needs next.
problems.statement:
Write flatten(nested) as a generator that yields every non-list element inside nested, at any depth, left to right.

This is deliberately the same shape as walking every leaf of a tree -- just on plain nested lists instead of Node objects. The trap is the same one too: calling flatten(item) on a line by itself creates a generator and throws it away without yielding anything. You need yield from to forward what an inner call produces.
hints: Use yield, never build and return a list. Loop over nested: for each item, check isinstance(item, list).
If item is a plain value, yield item directly. If item is a list, you need everything it eventually yields, at whatever depth -- that's yield from flatten(item).
Writing flatten(item) alone (no yield, no yield from) on its own line does nothing observable -- it builds a generator object and immediately discards it without running any of its code.

tests.name: calling it returns a generator
tests.src:
import inspect
result = flatten([1, 2])
assert inspect.isgenerator(result), (
    "flatten returned %s -- use yield, not return" % type(result).__name__)

tests.name: flat and nested lists, left to right
tests.src:
assert list(flatten([1, [2, 3], 4])) == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert list(flatten([1, [2, [3, [4]]]])) == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert list(flatten([])) == []

tests.name: the first value arrives without walking the rest
tests.src:
class Poisoned(list):
    def __iter__(self):
        raise AssertionError(
            "the rest of the list was walked before the first value was "
            "requested -- yield as you go, using yield from on nested "
            "lists")

late = [2, 3]
tail = Poisoned([late])
gen = flatten([1] + tail)
assert next(gen) == 1

tests.name: random nested lists, checked against a direct flatten

problems.title: Where the Biggest Number Is, Not Just What It Is
problems.blurb: A recursive call that has to hand back two things at once, because one of them alone can't answer the question.
problems.statement:
Write index_of_max(values): the index of the largest value in a non-empty list. If several elements tie for largest, return the index of the first one.

This is the same problem as max_of_list, with one twist that changes everything about the recursion: you now need to report where the max is, not just what it is. A recursive call on values[1:] that only returns an index isn't enough on its own — you can't tell whether values[0] beats it without also knowing what value that index points to. And a call that only returns the value isn't enough either — you'd have the number but no position.

The fix is to have the recursive call return both the best value and its index together, as a pair, so every level of the recursion has everything it needs to make its own comparison. Only the outermost call needs to throw away the value and keep just the index — which is exactly why a small helper that returns the pair, called once from inside index_of_max, is the natural shape here.
hints: Write a helper, best(values), that returns (value, index) for the best element -- the index is relative to whatever list was passed to that call, not the original list.
Base case of the helper: one element left. Its pair is (values[0], 0).

Recursive case: rest_value, rest_index = best(values[1:]). If values[0] is at least as big as rest_value, this call's answer is (values[0], 0). Otherwise it's (rest_value, rest_index + 1) -- the +1 shifts the index because rest_index was counted from the start of the shorter, sliced list, one position to the right of where values[0] sits.

Use >=, not >, in that comparison. values[0] is always to the left of everything best(values[1:]) considered, so on an exact tie it must win -- using a strict > lets the rest of the list keep a later duplicate instead of yielding to the earlier one.
index_of_max itself is one line: call best(values) and return only the index half of the pair.

tests.name: a single element is at index 0
tests.src: assert index_of_max([7]) == 0

tests.name: the max in different positions
tests.src:
assert index_of_max([3, 9, 2]) == 1
assert index_of_max([9, 3, 2]) == 0
assert index_of_max([3, 2, 9]) == 2

tests.name: ties resolve to the first occurrence
tests.src:
got = index_of_max([1, 5, 5, 2])
assert got == 1, ("got %d -- a later tie replaced the earlier one, use a "
                  "strict > comparison" % got)
got = index_of_max([5, 1, 5])
assert got == 0, got

tests.name: all negative values
tests.src: assert index_of_max([-5, -1, -9]) == 1

tests.name: random lists, checked against a direct scan

problems.title: Two Recursive Calls, Combined
problems.blurb: Branching recursion: each call spawns two more, the same way a tree node's children each spawn their own subtrees.
problems.statement:
Write fibonacci(n): the nth Fibonacci number, where fibonacci(0) = 0, fibonacci(1) = 1, and every later term is the sum of the two before it. Assume n >= 0.

Every problem so far had one recursive call per branch. This one has two — fibonacci(n - 1) and fibonacci(n - 2) — combined into one answer, the same way a tree node with several children combines each child's separately computed result. Getting comfortable with "make more than one recursive call, then combine what comes back" is the last piece before moving on to trees, where a node can have any number of children, not just two.

This one also has two base cases, not one — both fibonacci(0) and fibonacci(1) are answered directly, without recursing.
hints: Two base cases: n == 0 returns 0, n == 1 returns 1. Handle both before anything recursive.
For n >= 2: fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2). Each of those calls is trusted to already be correct on its own -- you don't need to trace through either one by hand.

This is slow for large n because the same smaller value gets recomputed many times across the branches -- that's fine for this problem, and it's exactly the same cost tradeoff an unpruned game tree has.

tests.name: both base cases
tests.src:
assert fibonacci(0) == 0
assert fibonacci(1) == 1

tests.name: the first several terms
tests.src:
assert fibonacci(2) == 1
assert fibonacci(3) == 2
assert fibonacci(4) == 3
assert fibonacci(5) == 5
assert fibonacci(6) == 8

tests.name: checked against a direct iterative computation

problems.title: Reversing a String, One Character at a Time
problems.blurb: sum_list's exact shape, on characters instead of numbers.
problems.statement:
Write reverse_string(s) recursively, without slicing the whole string backwards (s[::-1]) and without a loop.

Same shape as sum_list: peel off one piece (s[0]), trust the recursive call to correctly handle everything after it (s[1:]), then decide where the peeled piece goes relative to that trusted result.
hints: Base case: the empty string reverses to itself.
reverse_string(s[1:]) already correctly reverses everything after the first character. Where does s[0] belong relative to that already-reversed piece -- the front of it, or the back?
return reverse_string(s[1:]) + s[0].

tests.name: empty and single character
tests.src:
assert reverse_string("") == ""
assert reverse_string("a") == "a"

tests.name: short strings
tests.src:
assert reverse_string("abc") == "cba"
assert reverse_string("hello") == "olleh"

tests.name: random strings, checked against slicing

problems.title: Palindromes, From Both Ends at Once
problems.blurb: A base case with two exits, and a recursive case that shrinks from both sides.
problems.statement:
Write is_palindrome(s): whether s reads the same forwards and backwards, recursively.

Unlike the earlier problems, the recursive step here strips one character off each end at once, rather than peeling off just the first. That means there are two ways to reach a base case: a string can shrink down to a single character, or it can shrink down to nothing (from an even-length string). Both are trivially palindromes.
problems.examples:
>>> is_palindrome("")
True
>>> is_palindrome("a")
True
>>> is_palindrome("racecar")
True
>>> is_palindrome("hello")
False
hints: Base cases: len(s) <= 1 is always a palindrome -- nothing left to compare.
Otherwise: does s[0] match s[-1]? If not, you already know the answer is False without recursing at all.
If the ends do match, the whole string is a palindrome exactly when the middle -- s[1:-1] -- is also a palindrome. That's the recursive call.

tests.name: the base cases
tests.src:
assert is_palindrome("") is True
assert is_palindrome("a") is True

tests.name: even and odd length palindromes
tests.src:
assert is_palindrome("racecar") is True
assert is_palindrome("abba") is True

tests.name: non-palindromes, including a near miss
tests.src:
assert is_palindrome("hello") is False
assert is_palindrome("abcba ") is False

tests.name: random strings, checked against slicing
tests.src:
import random, string
random.seed(12)
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(0, 8)
    s = "".join(random.choice("ab") for _ in range(n))
    assert is_palindrome(s) == (s == s[::-1]), s

problems.title: Exponentiation, Recursively
problems.blurb: Two arguments this time -- and only one of them shrinks toward the base case.
problems.statement:
Write power(base, exponent), computing base ** exponent recursively, for exponent >= 0, without using ** or a loop.

This has two parameters, but only exponent moves toward a base case -- base stays fixed across every recursive call. That is completely normal: not every argument needs to shrink, only enough of them to guarantee the recursion eventually stops.
hints: Base case: anything to the power 0 is 1.
Recursive case: power(base, exponent - 1) already correctly computes base ** (exponent - 1). Multiply that trusted result by base once more to get base ** exponent.
base itself is never passed anything different across the recursive calls -- it's exponent that counts down to the base case.

tests.name: the base case
tests.src:
assert power(2, 0) == 1
assert power(-7, 0) == 1

tests.name: small exponents
tests.src:
assert power(2, 5) == 32
assert power(5, 1) == 5
assert power(3, 3) == 27

tests.name: negative bases
tests.src: assert power(-2, 3) == -8

tests.name: random bases and exponents, checked against **
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(13)
for _ in range(200):
    base = random.randint(-10, 10)
    exponent = random.randint(0, 8)
    assert power(base, exponent) == base ** exponent, (base, exponent)

problems.title: Greatest Common Divisor, the Euclidean Way
problems.blurb: The recursive call gets a transformed pair, not a smaller slice -- a new kind of shrinking.
problems.statement:
Write gcd(a, b) for non-negative integers, using Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, 0) is a, and otherwise gcd(a, b) equals gcd(b, a % b).

Every earlier problem shrank its input by removing one element or subtracting one from a count. This one shrinks differently: the pair (a, b) becomes the pair (b, a % b), and b is guaranteed to strictly decrease each time (since a % b < b), which is what guarantees the recursion still reaches b == 0 eventually.
hints: Base case: b == 0. The answer is just a.
Recursive case: return gcd(b, a % b). Notice the arguments swap places -- the old second argument becomes the new first one.
Trust that gcd(b, a % b) is already correct; you don't combine its result with anything else here, you just return it directly.

tests.name: one argument already zero
tests.src:
assert gcd(9, 0) == 9
assert gcd(0, 9) == 9
assert gcd(0, 0) == 0

tests.name: small pairs
tests.src:
assert gcd(12, 8) == 4
assert gcd(17, 5) == 1
assert gcd(100, 75) == 25

tests.name: random pairs, checked against math.gcd
tests.src:
import random, math
random.seed(14)
for _ in range(300):
    a = random.randint(0, 500)
    b = random.randint(0, 500)
    assert gcd(a, b) == math.gcd(a, b), (a, b)

problems.title: Summing an Integer's Digits
problems.blurb: Shrinking an integer with // and % instead of slicing a list.
problems.statement:
Write digit_sum(n) for n >= 0: the sum of its decimal digits, recursively, without converting it to a string.

There's no list or string to slice here, so the recursive step needs a different way to peel off "the last piece and everything else": n % 10 is the last digit, and n // 10 is every digit before it, as a smaller integer.
hints: Base case: n == 0. There are no digits left to add, but be careful -- digit_sum(0) itself, as a top-level call, should still give 0, not skip a real digit that happens to be 0.
Recursive case: n % 10 is the last digit. n // 10 is the number with that last digit removed -- strictly smaller, moving toward the base case.
return n % 10 + digit_sum(n // 10).

tests.name: zero and single digits
tests.src:
assert digit_sum(0) == 0
assert digit_sum(7) == 7

tests.name: multi-digit numbers
tests.src:
assert digit_sum(123) == 6
assert digit_sum(9999) == 36
assert digit_sum(1000) == 1

tests.name: random numbers, checked against a string-based sum
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(15)
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(0, 10 ** 6)
    assert digit_sum(n) == sum(int(c) for c in str(n)), n

problems.title: Cutting the List in Half Each Time
problems.blurb: Every earlier problem shrank by one element. This one shrinks by half.
problems.statement:
Write binary_search(values, target): given a list sorted in increasing order, return the index of target, or -1 if it isn't present.

Every recursive problem so far shrank its input by removing exactly one element (values[1:], n - 1, one character off an end). This one shrinks by throwing away half the list every call -- the reason binary search is fast. Slicing a list is possible but wasteful here (it copies half the list every call); track the search window instead with a low and high index into the original list, and shrink the gap between them.
hints: Base case: low > high means the window is empty -- nothing left to check, target isn't here. Return -1.
Otherwise look at the midpoint: mid = (low + high) // 2. If values[mid] == target, you're done -- return mid directly, no recursion needed.

If values[mid] is too small, the target (if present) must be to the right: recurse on search(mid + 1, high). If it's too big, recurse on search(low, mid - 1). Either way the window is at least half the previous size.

tests.name: empty list
tests.src: assert binary_search([], 5) == -1

tests.name: found at various positions
tests.src:
values = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
assert binary_search(values, 7) == 3
assert binary_search(values, 1) == 0
assert binary_search(values, 9) == 4

tests.name: not present, including gaps and out of range
tests.src:
values = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
assert binary_search(values, 4) == -1
assert binary_search(values, 0) == -1
assert binary_search(values, 100) == -1

tests.name: random sorted lists, checked against a linear scan

problems.title: Checking Order, One Adjacent Pair at a Time
problems.blurb: A recursive AND -- the whole list is sorted only if every piece agrees.
problems.statement:
Write is_sorted(values): whether the list is in non-decreasing order, recursively, without a loop.

The list is sorted exactly when its first two elements are in order and everything from the second element onward is also sorted. That "and" is doing real work: both halves have to hold, so a single False anywhere should make the whole answer False, however early it's found.
problems.examples:
>>> is_sorted([])
True
>>> is_sorted([5])
True
>>> is_sorted([1, 2, 2, 5])
True
>>> is_sorted([3, 1, 2])
False
hints: Base case: a list with 0 or 1 elements has no adjacent pair to violate order, so it's trivially sorted.
Recursive case: check values[0] <= values[1]. If that's already False, the whole list is unsorted -- no need to look further.
If the first pair is fine, the answer depends entirely on whether values[1:] is sorted: return values[0] <= values[1] and is_sorted(values[1:]).

tests.name: the base cases
tests.src:
assert is_sorted([]) is True
assert is_sorted([5]) is True

tests.name: sorted lists, with and without duplicates
tests.src:
assert is_sorted([1, 2, 2, 5]) is True
assert is_sorted([1, 1, 1]) is True

tests.name: unsorted, including a violation only at the very end
tests.src:
assert is_sorted([3, 1, 2]) is False
assert is_sorted([1, 2, 3, 4, 2]) is False

tests.name: random lists, checked against sorted()
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(17)
for _ in range(300):
    values = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10))]
    assert is_sorted(values) == (values == sorted(values)), values

problems.title: Dropping Repeats From a Sorted List
problems.blurb: Whether to keep the first element depends on what the recursive call decides to do with the second.
problems.statement:
Write remove_duplicates(values): given a list sorted in non-decreasing order, return a new list with consecutive duplicates collapsed down to one copy each.

The earlier list problems could look at values[0] in isolation. This one can't: whether to keep values[0] depends on whether it's equal to values[1] -- which means peeking one element ahead, not just delegating everything after the first element to the recursive call unseen.
hints: Base case: 0 or 1 elements. There's nothing that could be a duplicate of anything else, so return values unchanged.

Recursive case: rest = remove_duplicates(values[1:]) already correctly de-duplicates everything after the first element -- so rest[0], if rest is non-empty, is the next distinct value after values[0].
If values[0] == values[1], values[0] is a duplicate that should be dropped -- return rest as-is. Otherwise values[0] is a new distinct value -- return [values[0]] + rest.

tests.name: the base cases
tests.src:
assert remove_duplicates([]) == []
assert remove_duplicates([5]) == [5]

tests.name: runs of duplicates, and none at all
tests.src:
assert remove_duplicates([1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3]
assert remove_duplicates([1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3]

tests.name: every element the same
tests.src: assert remove_duplicates([4, 4, 4, 4]) == [4]

tests.name: random sorted lists, checked against a direct de-dup

problems.title: Every Subset: Include It, or Don't
problems.blurb: Two recursive calls representing a choice, not two halves of a computation -- the shape every backtracking search is built from.
problems.statement:
Write all_subsets(values), returning every subset of values (as a list of lists; order among the subsets does not matter). A list of n elements has 2 ** n subsets, including the empty one and the whole list itself.

fibonacci made two recursive calls and added their results together. This one also makes two recursive calls, but they mean something different: without_first is every subset that excludes values[0], and pairing values[0] onto the front of each of those same subsets gives every subset that includes it. Every subset falls into exactly one of those two groups, so the full answer is both groups combined.

This "include it, or don't, for every element" pattern is the foundation of backtracking search -- the same choice, made once per element, with recursion handling every combination of choices for you.
hints: Base case: the empty list has exactly one subset -- itself. Return [[]], a list containing one empty list -- not [], which would mean zero subsets.
Recursive case: without_first = all_subsets(values[1:]). That's every subset of the rest of the list, already computed, none of which contain values[0].

with_first = [[values[0]] + subset for subset in without_first] -- the same subsets, each with values[0] added on. Every real subset is in exactly one of the two groups, so the answer is with_first + without_first.

tests.name: the empty list has one subset: itself
tests.src: assert all_subsets([]) == [[]]

tests.name: small lists against the exact expected sets
the count is always 2**n, with no duplicates and no omissions
tests.src:
import itertools
for n in range(6):
    values = list(range(n))
    subsets = all_subsets(values)
    assert len(subsets) == 2 ** n, (n, len(subsets))
    as_sets = [frozenset(s) for s in subsets]
    assert len(set(as_sets)) == len(as_sets), "a subset was produced twice"
    want = {frozenset(c) for k in range(n + 1)
           for c in itertools.combinations(values, k)}
    assert set(as_sets) == want, values

problems.title: Towers of Hanoi: the Move List Itself
problems.blurb: Two recursive calls, both used -- and the answer is built by gluing three pieces together, not by comparing or summing them.
problems.statement:
Move n disks from peg source to peg target, using a third peg spare, one disk at a time, never placing a bigger disk on a smaller one. Write hanoi_moves(n, source, target, spare), returning the full list of moves as (from_peg, to_peg) pairs, in order.

The classic insight: to move n disks from source to target, first move the top n - 1 disks out of the way onto spare (using target as the extra space during that detour), then move the one big disk directly from source to target, then move those n - 1 disks from spare onto target (using source as the extra space this time).

That's two recursive calls again, like all_subsets -- but this time neither call's result gets compared or filtered. Both lists of moves are used in full, concatenated together around the one move in the middle.

hints: Base case: n == 0. No disks to move, so the list of moves is empty.
Recursive case, three pieces glued together in order: hanoi_moves(n - 1, source, spare, target) -- notice target and spare swap roles here, since target is the extra space during this detour.
Then one move of your own: (source, target). Then hanoi_moves(n - 1, spare, target, source) -- here source becomes the extra space. Concatenate all three with +.

tests.name: zero disks is no moves at all
tests.src: assert hanoi_moves(0, "A", "C", "B") == []

tests.name: one and two disks against the exact expected moves
tests.src:
assert hanoi_moves(1, "A", "C", "B") == [("A", "C")]
assert hanoi_moves(2, "A", "C", "B") == [
    ("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C")]

tests.name: the move count is always 2**n - 1
every move is legal: no disk ever lands on a smaller one
